title: Reedbeds and Rip Currents: The Danube Delta and the Romanian Coast by Paddle
subRegion: The Danube Delta & the Dobrogea Coast

hook: Half of this week is spent below the reeds, in a kayak on channels where the horizon is two metres of *stuf* and the only sound is a coot. The other half is on a coast that runs from a lagoon full of kites to a scruffy, beloved village on the Bulgarian border. It is a trip of ferries you cannot rush, boatmen who know where the pelicans are, and a sea that has no tide but plenty of current.

snapshot.Difficulty: Moderate (flatwater paddling, 10–20 km days, no whitewater)
snapshot.Start / End: Tulcea → Vama Veche (linear, delta then coast)
snapshot.Getting there: Bucharest Otopeni (OTP) to Tulcea is 260 km / 4 h by road or coach; Constanța (CND) has seasonal flights [VERIFY: current CND seasonal routes]. Go carless for the delta half and pick up a hire car in Tulcea or Constanța for the coast.

itinerary.title: Tulcea, paperwork and the waterfront (transfer day)
itinerary.morning: Travel from Bucharest to Tulcea, the delta's only real gateway town, and buy or collect the ARBDD access permit before doing anything else. Carry it on the water.
itinerary.afternoon: Check the Navrom Delta timetable in person at the passenger terminal. Classic slow ferries and faster boats run on fixed weekdays to Sulina, Sfântu Gheorghe and the Chilia line, and the pattern changes by season [VERIFY: current Navrom sailing days and departure times].
itinerary.evening: Walk the Tulcea quay and visit the Danube Delta Eco-Tourism Museum Centre for the aquarium of Danube fish. Eat by the water and buy repellent, sun cream and cash before you leave town.

itinerary.title: Down the Sulina arm to Crișan
itinerary.morning: Take the Navrom boat down the Sulina arm past Partizani and Maliuc. This is the working delta: dredgers, cargo, reed-cutters' barges and the occasional white-tailed eagle over the willows.
itinerary.afternoon: Land at Crișan and take a kayak straight onto the Dunărea Veche, the Old Danube, the abandoned meander that loops behind the village. Pure flatwater, high reed walls, and terns working the channel.
itinerary.evening: Stay at Ivan Pescar in Crișan, a fisherman's pensiune on the bank [VERIFY: current rates and board arrangement]. Dinner is *borș de pește* or fried carp; the delta eats what it caught that day.

itinerary.title: The Crișan–Mila 23 canal
itinerary.morning: Paddle the Crișan–Mila 23 canal, the classic delta kayak line: a straight cut that opens into the Old Danube's meanders, with pelican rafts on the wider stretches in the early hours.
itinerary.afternoon: Reach Mila 23, a Lipovan fishing village of one street, painted boats and Russian spoken at the fence line. The village produced Romania's canoeing dynasty; the boats on the bank are still working craft.
itinerary.evening: Return by paddle or arrange a lift back with a local boat. Sunset over Lake Roșu, reached from the Mila 23 side, is the delta's stock photograph for a reason.

itinerary.title: Caraorman, Letea and why you need a boatman (guided boat day)
itinerary.morning: Hire a local boatman rather than navigating alone. The channels toward Caraorman are unmarked, silt seasonally and dead-end into private fishing grounds; a Crișan or Mila 23 driver knows which cut is open this month [VERIFY: current guided-boat day rate].
itinerary.afternoon: Caraorman's sand dunes and old oak stand sit behind the village, an inland dune field in the middle of a wetland. Letea, the older and stranger forest with its feral horses, is the northern equivalent and is entered only with a licensed guide on marked routes.
itinerary.evening: Take the ferry or a boat transfer down to Sulina. The town is Romania's easternmost, an old free port that shrank; nothing is quick to reach and that is part of it.

itinerary.title: Sulina, Mile 0 and the sea
itinerary.morning: Walk to Mile 0, where the Sulina arm is measured out into the sea between two long jetties. The old lighthouse in town, once at the waterline, now stands several hundred metres inland — the river built the land beneath it.
itinerary.afternoon: The Maritime Cemetery holds British, Greek, Turkish and Russian graves from the Danube Commission era. Then cycle or walk east to Sulina beach, a wide unguarded strand where the freshwater plume meets the sea.
itinerary.evening: Eat at a Sulina fish table — La Cherhana is the name to ask for, cherhana being the old fish-landing station [VERIFY: current location and hours]. Watch the pilot boats work the mouth.

itinerary.title: Sfântu Gheorghe and out to the coast
itinerary.morning: Boat south to Sfântu Gheorghe, the delta's third arm and its most isolated village, where the Danube ends in a shifting sandbar. Green Village is the established stay if you break the journey here [VERIFY: current rates and open season].
itinerary.afternoon: Walk or take the village tractor-trailer 2 km to the wild beach: unguarded, enormous, with strong outflow current where the arm meets the sea. Swim inshore of the bar, not across it.
itinerary.evening: Ferry back to Tulcea, collect a car and drive south past Corbu's wild beach and the Năvodari lagoon to Mamaia. Pensiunea Delta Marina is a practical Tulcea-side fallback if the ferry runs late [VERIFY: current operation and location].

itinerary.title: Siutghiol, then the southern villages
itinerary.morning: Rig on Lake Siutghiol behind Mamaia. Flat water, steady onshore breeze from mid-morning, and a lagoon big enough to ride out without crossing shipping. Beginners take the lagoon; the sea side is for swell days.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive south through Costinești, the old student resort, to 2 Mai and Vama Veche — two villages a kilometre from the Bulgarian border that have been Romania's alternative summer for fifty years. Casa Coral and Stuf Vama Veche are the recognised beds [VERIFY: current operation and rates].
itinerary.evening: Grilled fish, a guitar, and a beach that is unguarded at both ends. Constanța is 50 km back north for the airport, or Bucharest 300 km on the A2 — about three hours.

accommodationStrategy.name: Ivan Pescar
accommodationStrategy.description: on the bank of the Sulina arm at the exact point where the Old Danube and the Mila 23 canal both begin, so both kayak days start from the jetty. Boat, kayak and local knowledge come with the house.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct by phone 4–6 weeks ahead for May–June; confirm whether the rate is half or full board, because there is no alternative kitchen.

accommodationStrategy.name: Green Village
accommodationStrategy.description: the only substantial accommodation in the most isolated of the three arms, with its own boat transfers and reliable food. It makes the wild beach and the Sacalin sandbar area viable without camping.
accommodationStrategy.booking: well ahead for the August film-festival week; the operating season is shorter than the calendar suggests [VERIFY: current season dates].

accommodationStrategy.name: Stuf Vama Veche
accommodationStrategy.description: walkable to the beach and to every table in the village, which matters because Vama Veche is a walking-and-drinking place, not a driving one. Simple, cheap, loud in August, calm in September.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3–5 weeks for September; August is a domestic scramble and worth avoiding entirely.

logistics.connectivity: 4G covers Tulcea, Crișan, Sulina and Sfântu Gheorghe but drops out on the channels between them. Download offline charts; the delta's canals are poorly rendered on standard map apps.
logistics.emergency: 112. In the delta, response comes by boat and is slow — tell your pensiune your paddling plan and expected return, and carry a whistle and a dry-bagged phone.
logistics.weather: the delta is flat and exposed. A sudden squall raises short, steep chop on Lake Roșu and the wide channels within minutes. Get into a reed-sheltered cut rather than trying to cross open water.
logistics.bookingWindows: May–June and September pensiuni need 4–6 weeks. Boatmen are arranged the day before, in person, through your host — not online.
logistics.money: Romanian lei. Tulcea, Constanța and Mamaia take cards everywhere; the delta villages largely do not. Draw 1,500–2,000 RON in Tulcea for boatmen, permits, tips and village purchases.
logistics.transportRules: a *rovinietă* road vignette is required in Romania — hire cars usually include it; confirm. Navrom ferries carry bicycles and kayaks for a supplement and cannot be booked far in advance; arrive at the terminal early.
logistics.permits: the ARBDD permit is compulsory and checked. Strictly protected zones are closed outright, no fires or wild camping outside designated spots, no approaching bird colonies, and fishing requires its own separate licence. Rangers do patrol.

proTips: Paddle between 06:00 and 09:00. Wind is nil, the channels are glass, pelicans and herons are feeding, and by 11:00 the tour boats have pushed everything into cover.
Buy the ARBDD permit before you reach the water, not after a ranger asks. Enforcement is real and the fine costs far more than the permit.
Take a boatman for one full day even if you paddle the rest. The difference between seeing the delta and finding the delta is entirely local knowledge of which cut is open.
Bring a head net, long sleeves and DEET even in June. Evening on a Crișan terrace in still air is not survivable in shorts.
Ride the classic slow Navrom ferry in at least one direction. It is cheaper than the fast boat, it stops at villages the fast boat skips, and it is the way the delta actually travels.
On the coast, go to Vama Veche in September rather than August. Same village, a tenth of the crowd, and the sea is warmer than it was in June.

raw.Prevailing wind: Summer on the Dobrogea coast runs a north-easterly to easterly sea breeze that fills through the afternoon — light in the morning, 12–20 knots from mid-afternoon, fading at dusk. September adds the first synoptic northerlies, stronger and more consistent, which is when Mamaia's lagoon works best. Winter's *crivăț* from the north-east is out of season but explains the local rigging habits.
raw.Launch spots: On the sea side, Lake Siutghiol behind the Mamaia strip is the region's flat-water kite and wing venue — shallow, no swell, onshore breeze across a 5 km lagoon, and far more forgiving than the open beach two hundred metres away on the other side of the road. The Năvodari end of the lagoon and Corbu's wild beach take the overflow. In the delta, kayaks launch from Crișan's waterfront, Mila 23 and Sfântu Gheorghe.
raw.Equipment and hubs: Mamaia's watersports strip runs kite, wing and SUP schools through the summer season with English instruction [VERIFY: current Mamaia school rates and season dates]. In the delta, most pensiuni either keep kayaks or will call the neighbour who does; Crișan and Mila 23 are the reliable hire points, and a hired local boat with a driver is the standard way to reach anything beyond paddling range.
raw.Tidal and current awareness: The Black Sea is effectively non-tidal: the astronomical range is a few centimetres, so tide tables are irrelevant to launching, landing or beach camping here. The real hazards are wind-driven longshore currents that sweep parallel to shore on any sustained cross-shore breeze, rip currents off the long sandy bays at Corbu, Năvodari, Mamaia and Sfântu Gheorghe, and seiches — basin-scale oscillations that shift water level and flow inside enclosed bays. In the delta the current is riverine and constant: the Sulina arm runs hard and carries commercial traffic, so paddle the side channels and cross the main arm square, quickly and only with a clear sightline.
raw.Permits, mosquitoes and wildlife: Every visitor to the Danube Delta Biosphere Reserve needs an ARBDD access permit, and it is cheap rather than bureaucratic: **5 RON (about €1) per person per day, 15 RON (about €3) per person per week, 30 RON (about €6) per person per year** under Order 610/2009, with children, students and pensioners exempt along with residents of the reserve and its adjacent communes. A car needs its own permit — **10 RON per day or 100 RON per year** — and a private boat **20 RON per stay or 100 RON per year** (HG 538/2015). Buy online at permise.ddbra.ro, by SMS to **7494**, from the ARBDD permit machines in Tulcea and the delta villages and at SelfPay terminals nationwide, or over the counter at ARBDD headquarters in Tulcea (Mon–Thu 08:00–16:30, Fri 08:00–14:00) and the information centres at Chilia Veche, Sulina, Crișan and Murighiol. Rangers check it on the water — carry the SMS or the printout. A tour operator's boat fare does not include your personal permit unless they say so in writing. Strictly protected zones — Roșca-Buhaiova, the Letea and Caraorman cores, Sacalin-Zătoane, Periteașca-Leahova among them — are closed to visitors entirely, with no permit that opens them. Great white and Dalmatian pelicans nest here; both are strictly protected and you must not approach, circle or flush a raft of birds — keep several hundred metres and let them drift to you. Mosquitoes in July and August are genuinely brutal after 18:00; May, June and September are the reason to come then.
